title: Reeve Farm Site
summary: The Reeve Farm Site is remembered through the disturbance, collection, and public display of Native ancestral remains uncovered in Aquebogue in 1961. The episode shows how farming, collecting, archaeological interpretation, and museum display harmed Native ancestors and why burial protection remains necessary.
map_geometry_source: Broad public orientation point for Aquebogue from OSM/Nominatim and Directus text; not the farm, parcel, or ancestral remains location.
why_this_matters: The 1961 discovery of ancestral remains at the Reeve Farm Site led to decades of amateur looting and the insensitive public display of Indigenous ancestors at a local historical society. Recognizing this history of disrespectful treatment highlights the critical importance of modern repatriation efforts and the necessity of treating Native American resting places with care and cultural respect rather than as historical curiosities.
history_content:
In 1961, plowing at Reeve Farm exposed Native ancestral remains. Digging followed, and the remains of a young woman and child were removed. Public attention brought people onto the farm to search for belongings, further disturbing the land.

The remains were sold to the Bridgehampton Historical Museum, displayed, moved into storage, and transferred to the Southold Indian Museum, where a 1982 newspaper report announced their return to exhibition. That article also repeated an archaeological interpretation of the child's death as a general Native custom. The available evidence does not support that generalization, and it should not be presented as fact about Indigenous family life.
